newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION-Goldman Sachs on German economic reform.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Goldman Sachs on German economic reform.

text.p: By Thomas Meyer, senior international economist at Goldman, Sachs & Co oHG, in Frankfurt
THE FRUITS OF REFORM ARE RIPENING SLOWLY

During recent years the view that comprehensive reform in the German economy is necessary has grown. In particular, corporate restructuring has made clear advances. By contrast the restructuring of the public sector has been modest. However, a number of politicians are beginning to lose patience because of continuing growth in joblessness. Calls on industry to start hiring again are getting louder and the danger of a disappointing outcome to the programme of reform is getting greater. It is also not being recognised that it will take years before the slow implementation of further reforms will bear fruit in the form of higher growth and lower unemployment.

To judge just how long the process of reform will take, it is worthwhile looking at the experiences of the United States. The mistakes of the 1970s became clearly visible in the first half of the 1980s. Firstly, U.S. companies did not learn to closely monitor their production costs during the period of high inflation in the 1970s. It was too easy to just transfer their higher costs into higher prices. Secondly, they got used to measuring the success of their businesses by the size of the balance sheet rather than measuring it in terms of return on capital invested. Thirdly when dealing with investment there was too much emphasis on tax aspects rather than productive investments and innovation. The strong rise in the U.S. dollar, which peaked in 1985, was another factor in reducing the international competitiveness of U.S. companies and which caused many sectors of U.S. industry to fall into crisis.

The crisis brought about by the dollar's rise peaked in 1985, which also marked the turnaround. In the following years U.S. companies made extreme efforts to master the problem. Cost control, optimisation of inventory, high investment, technical upgrades and increasing capital yields became the most important corporate goals. The restructuring of companies to reach these goals was backed up with comprehensive political reforms. Soon after taking over office at the start of the 1980s, the Reagan administration cut taxes, reduced the power of the unions and introduced the deregulation of a larger number of sectors in the economy. A comprehensive reform of the tax system came in the middle of the 1980s. The level of growth in the U.S. economy during the 1980s was not bad. However, it was not until the start of the current upswing in 1991 -- around six years after the high-point of the crisis -- that the fruits of restructuring and reform in the form of strong growth and higher employment, combined with simul

Looked at overall, the problems of the U.S. economy in the middle of the 1980s are very similar to those of the German economy in the mid-1990s. In Germany we can date the peak of the structural crisis to the start of 1995. At this time the IG Metall union secured a pay rise of 10 percent for the time between December 1994 and December 1995 and the deutschemark rose to a value of 1.35 to the dollar. The postive cost shock and negative price shock from this brought the German economy round on a wider front. After initial delay, reform proposals in economic policy began in 1996. If we assume that the German reform process develops at the same pace as that in the U.S., one could say that German reforms in 1997 are at around the levels of those in the U.S. in 1987. If the German economy follows the American example, then we can expect the first fruits of reform from the year 2001.

There are no reasons to speculate that the German reform process will be slower than that of the U.S. in the 1980s. The German economy even has the advantage that it can follow the American example. But it also a number of handicaps: the power of the unions in Germany is unbroken. The unions have it in their power to delay the process of reform. Secondly, political reforms only come extremely slowly in Germany, because political parties oppose them. Thirdly, the German public is afraid of change and technical improvement. All of these leave one to presume that the restructuring of the German economy will take longer than the American.

The long thirsty stretch between the start of the reform process and the first taste of the fruits of reform means there is a danger that politicians, especially, will lose patience and abandon the straight road to reform. The short term relief which abandoning the course of reform would bring to the electorate would have to be paid for in the long term by a further uncontrolled decline in the economic situation.
